modules.description: What turns a good shift into a job you keep: handing a ticket over so the next person can act immediately, agreeing what the support engagement actually covers, and showing a hiring client evidence rather than adjectives.

lessons.title: Escalation as a handoff
lessons.content_mdx:
# Escalation as a handoff

Chapter one said escalation is the right answer to a question above your seat, not a failure. This lesson is the other half. How you hand a ticket over decides whether the customer waits an hour or a day.

## What "pls help" costs

Marilou runs the chat queue for an online mattress store in Iloilo. A customer messages that the bed frame arrived with a cracked slat. Replacing a part is not something Marilou can approve, so she screenshots the chat, drops it in the team channel with "pls help po", and opens the next ticket.

She has handed her supervisor a puzzle. He has to find the order, read the whole thread, work out what Marilou already told the customer, check whether anything was promised, and guess what she wants him to do. That takes longer than answering it himself would have taken, and the customer sits through all of it.

An escalation is not passing the problem along. It is passing a decision, with everything needed to make it already attached.

## The five lines

Write the handoff as one block at the top of the ticket, in this order.

1. **What the customer asked for**, in their words, trimmed to the request.
2. **What I have already told them.** Copy it exactly if you promised anything.
3. **What I checked and ruled out.** Order status, earlier tickets, the policy line you read, the detail you verified.
4. **What I think should happen.** A recommendation, not a question.
5. **What has been promised, and by when.**

Marilou's version:

> Customer received the frame with a cracked slat, wants the slat replaced, does not want to return the whole bed. Order verified, delivered Tuesday, photo attached, no earlier tickets on this order. I have told her we are checking and that she will hear from us before I log off today. I have offered her nothing. My read: send a replacement slat, no pickup needed. Needs your approval.

A supervisor can answer that in a single read.

The line new agents leave out is the recommendation. It is also the line that gets you trusted. Being wrong about it costs you nothing, because the person you asked is the one deciding. Having no view at all is what makes you look like a relay.

## Drafting the handoff without handing over the customer

A long thread is the kind of thing a model summarises well, so use it. Strip the ticket first, the way chapter one had you strip the queue: no name, no address, no order reference, no pasted customer text. Give it the situation in your own words and ask for lines one, two and three of the shape above.

Then write line four yourself. Every other line can be checked against the thread, so a paraphrased promise or a misread request gets caught on the read. The recommendation cannot be checked against anything, because it is not in the thread. It is your view, it is the line that gets you trusted, and a model producing one has no stake in whether it is right.

## Escalated does not mean no longer mine

The ticket stays yours until somebody says, in writing, that they have it. A status field is not a person.

Set your own reminder to check on it, and check before the time you promised the customer, not after. If the person you escalated to works while you sleep, plan around that rather than hoping. Decide what you will send the customer if the answer has not arrived, and write it before you need it.

## The holding reply

The customer does not care which desk the ticket is sitting on. They care whether they have been forgotten.

Three parts: what has happened so far, what is happening now, and when they hear from you next. The third part does the work, and it has to be a time you can hit even if nothing is resolved by then. If the answer is not in, you send another short note at that time. That is not an admission of failure. It is the thing that stops a patient customer turning into the angry repeat contact from chapter three.

> Hi Ms Ramos, I have your photo and your order shows as delivered Tuesday. A replacement slat needs approval from the warehouse and I have sent that across with your details. I will message you again before five today either way, even if the approval is still pending.

## Close the loop in your own words

When the approval comes back, do not assume anybody told the customer. Somebody fixing a thing is not the same as the customer knowing it was fixed, and a ticket quietly marked resolved is how a good ending turns into a complaint.

Send the confirmation yourself: what was done, what it means for them, and anything you still need from them. Then write down the answer you were given. The next time this ticket arrives, and it will arrive again, it may sit inside your seat, or it may become the next entry in the macro library from chapter two.

## Do this before the next lesson

Take a ticket you would have to escalate and write the five lines for it. Then read line four back. If it is a question rather than a recommendation, rewrite it as a recommendation.

lessons.title: Agreeing what the support job covers
lessons.content_mdx:
# Agreeing what the support job covers

Support scope rarely changes in one big request. It changes in small friendly ones, and every one of them is easy to say yes to.

## Four things settled before the first shift

**Which channels.** Email and a website chat widget is one job. Email, chat widget, the Facebook page inbox, Instagram DMs and a marketplace chat is a different job, with five sets of habits and five places to miss something. Write the list down and treat anything not on it as new work.

**Which hours.** Name the window you are at the queue, and name whose clock it runs on. If your client is overseas, agree the window in your own local time and let them translate it, because the gap between your clock and theirs shifts during their year. Chapter one covered what a queue promises and what happens to a ticket that lands outside coverage. This is where you write that answer down before it happens rather than after.

**Roughly what volume, and what happens above it.** Ask what the queue has been running at recently, and ask where that count came from. If nobody has a number, say you will measure the first month and bring it back. Either way you now have a baseline, and a baseline is the only thing that turns "parang mas mabigat na" into a conversation somebody can act on.

**What you are authorised to decide.** The list from chapter one, in writing, with the name of the person you ask when the list runs out.

## How creep arrives in a queue

Four shapes, and none of them looks like a demand.

- **The extra channel.** "Pwede mo rin ba i-check ang IG? Konti lang naman."
- **The new product line.** Same inbox, new questions, and your macros are quoting things that are no longer true.
- **Weekend cover, just this once.** Then the next sale. Then every sale.
- **Becoming the escalation point.** Questions you were hired to escalate start coming back to you, because by month three you know the answer. It is flattering, it is a promotion nobody agreed to, and it is the one that eats your day.

Analyn moved off a BPO floor in Cubao to run support for a skincare shop in Quezon City. She agreed to email and the page inbox. By week six she was also answering the Shopee chat and a Viber group, because each one was a small yes.

## Naming the change without refusing it

You are not turning work down. You are pricing it in time.

The move itself belongs to Client Communication in English: agree in principle, then name what it changes, then hand the client the choice. What a queue adds is the count. Analyn cannot say the IG inbox is heavy. She has to say what it is, in messages a day, and what it does to the email queue's first reply. Without the count it is a complaint. With it, it is an operations question the client can answer.

Then set a point to look again: after a launch, after a sale, after a price change, or on a date in the calendar. A ticket count from a campaign month is not the count for an ordinary month, and agreeing to revisit is far easier before you need it.

## The shape of the pay conversation

No figures here, and no rates. What matters at this stage is knowing which shape you are on, because each one breaks differently when the queue doubles.

- **Paid for hours worked.** Twice the tickets inside the same hours means you get busier and earn the same. Quality is the first thing that gives.
- **Paid for coverage**, meaning you are available across an agreed window. Same exposure as hours when volume climbs, but quiet weeks are paid too, which suits a queue that swings.
- **Paid by volume**, per ticket or per band of tickets. Pay follows the queue, and you carry the quiet months. A queue of simple questions and a queue of furious ones pay the same, so agree what counts as a ticket.

None of the three is the right one. Pick knowingly, and write down the trigger for revisiting it: a volume number, a new channel, or a date. What to charge is a different subject. What to agree on is this one.

## Do this before the next lesson

Write the four things you would settle before a first shift, in the words you would actually send a client. Mark the one you would be likeliest to leave vague.

lessons.title: Proving you can run a queue
lessons.content_mdx:
# Proving you can run a queue

Two people apply to run the same inbox. Both did support for eight months. One writes "excellent communication skills, hardworking, fast learner, can work under pressure". The other writes "I ran the email and page inbox for a skincare shop from March to August. Here is the triage sheet I worked from, three of my macros, one refusal I had to send, and the escalation note that went with it."

Only one of those can be checked. That is why only one of them is worth reading.

## Say only the numbers you can source

Support work produces numbers, and numbers are where support portfolios fall apart. Quote one and the next question is where it came from. If you cannot answer that in a sentence, everything else you said gets re-read with suspicion.

So keep the rule narrow. Say a number only when you can name three things: what it counts, the window it covers, and where you got it.

- Tickets you handled between two dates, counted from the helpdesk export or from your own log.
- Your first reply time, if the tool records it and you can point at where it appears.
- How many of your tickets came back after you closed them, counted the same way each week.

Be honest with yourself about what each one proves. Volume proves stamina and says nothing about quality. A fast first reply proves you were at the desk, not that anything got solved. Tickets that did not come back is the closest thing to a quality signal you own, and only if you can say how you counted it.

A metric you cannot show the source of is worth less than no metric at all.

If you never measured, do not reach for a figure you half remember, and do not borrow a benchmark out of an article about the support industry. Chapter one made the point already: the target on your queue was set by whoever runs that business, so the only numbers that mean anything are that queue's and yours. Open a sheet this week with the date, the count and the source, and in a month you will have something true to say.

## Read your own sent replies before anyone else does

Once a week, pull ten replies you sent and read them cold against a short rubric.

- Does the first line answer the question that was asked?
- Is every fact, figure, date and link in it something I checked?
- Did it promise only what my seat is allowed to grant?
- Does it say what happens next, and when?
- Would I be comfortable if the client read it aloud to the customer?

This is uncomfortable the first few times, and it is the cheapest improvement available to you, because it needs nobody's permission and no tool. It also builds the pack below, because the replies you are not embarrassed by are the ones worth showing.

## The pack that gets you shortlisted

Four artefacts, small enough for a busy person to read in five minutes.

1. **A triage sheet** for one queue: the categories, the rule for what gets answered first, and the two column split of what that seat may decide against what it must escalate.
2. **Two or three macros**, variable slots marked, with one shown filled in for a specific customer.
3. **One hard reply**, showing the AI draft and the version you actually sent, plus a line on what you changed and why.
4. **One escalation note**, in the five line shape from this chapter's first lesson.

Strip every real name, order number, phone number and address, and put placeholders in their place. Doing that properly, and the harder question of showing work covered by a confidentiality agreement, is a job hunting subject with its own course. If you have never been paid for support work, build the pack around a realistic queue and label it as a sample. A labelled sample is honest. A sample presented as a client is a lie you will be asked about in the interview.

## The mock ticket

Expect a hiring client to send one awkward ticket and ask what you would reply. They are not marking your grammar. They are reading for whether you answered the question, whether you promised something nobody gave you the authority to promise, whether you asked for the one detail you actually needed, and how you sound when the customer is unhappy.

The usual trap is an angry customer demanding a refund. Granting it is the failure. Answer the request, say what you would check, and add one line to the client underneath: "I have assumed a refund needs your approval. Tell me the real policy and I will adjust the reply." That line is the test.

More clients now send the ticket with their own tool's draft attached and ask what you would send. That is not a harder test, it is a clearer one, because they are watching you edit. What they are reading for is what you take out: the delivery date nobody confirmed, the refund nobody authorised, the paragraph of thanks sitting in front of the answer. Send back the cut version rather than a rewrite from scratch, and say in one line what you removed and why. A rewrite hides the edit they asked to see. On AI, one accurate sentence beats a tool name: you draft with it, and you read every reply before a customer does. AI Essentials for Work covers how to describe AI skills in general.

## Do this this week

Open a sheet with three columns: date, count, source. Then write the first artefact, the triage sheet, for the queue you would like to be running in six months. It is the shortest of the four and the one every other artefact hangs off. The assignment asks you for the rest.

quiz.prompt: Marilou cannot approve a replacement part, so she posts a screenshot of the chat in the team channel with "pls help po" and moves to her next ticket. What should she have sent instead?

options.text: A note with the request, what she has already told the customer, what she checked, and what she recommends
The screenshot plus the full chat history, so her supervisor has every detail and can decide however he wants
A short summary of the problem ending in a question asking her supervisor what he would like her to do next
The screenshot with the order number added, since her supervisor can pull the rest of the detail out himself

quiz.explanation: An escalation passes a decision, not a puzzle. The five lines let the next person act on one read: the request, what was already said, what was checked, your recommendation, and what has been promised. Handing over raw history makes them redo the work you already did, and a summary ending in a question leaves out the one line that gets you trusted.

quiz.prompt: You paste a stripped version of a long thread into a model and ask it to draft the five line handoff. Which of the five lines do you write yourself?

options.text: Line two, what you have already told the customer, because a model paraphrases and a promise has to be quoted exactly
Line four, your recommendation, because that is the line you are trusted for and a model has no stake in whether it is right
Line one, what the customer asked for, because a model reading a thread will pick the last complaint over the real request
None of them, as long as you read the whole draft back against the thread and correct anything in it that does not match

quiz.explanation: Every line gets checked against the thread, and that is exactly where a paraphrased promise or a misread ask gets caught. Line four is different in kind. There is nothing in the thread to check it against, because it is your view rather than a fact from the record. It is the line that makes you something other than a relay, being wrong about it costs you nothing, and a model producing one has no stake in it.

quiz.prompt: Jasper escalates a billing bug to the client's developer, sets the ticket status to Escalated, and moves on. Two days later the customer writes back asking whether anyone is still there. What went wrong?

options.text: Nothing in Jasper's handling, since the delay belongs to the developer who never acknowledged the ticket at all
He should have set himself a reminder to chase the developer, though the ticket was properly out of his hands
He escalated far too early, before the customer had asked for the problem to reach a technical person
He treated a status field as a handover, when the ticket was still his and the silence was his to prevent

quiz.explanation: Escalated does not mean no longer mine. A status is not a person accepting the ticket. It stays yours until somebody says in writing that they have it, which means you chase it and you keep the customer informed while it sits on another desk. A reminder to chase the developer is half the job, and it leaves the customer in exactly the silence she wrote about.

quiz.prompt: The supervisor approves the replacement slat, writes it in an internal note and marks the ticket resolved. Marilou sees the note. What does she do?

options.text: Leave it, since the ticket reads as resolved and the supervisor will have written to the customer when he approved it
Reopen it and ask the supervisor to tell the customer himself, since he is the one who made the decision
Message the customer herself with what was approved and what happens next, then log the answer she was given
Forward the supervisor's internal note to the customer so she can see for herself that the approval has come through

quiz.explanation: Somebody fixing a thing is not the same as the customer knowing it was fixed, and assuming the decider wrote to her is how a good ending turns into a complaint. An internal note is written for the team and carries wording that was never meant for her. Close the loop in your own words, then write down the answer, because that is what turns this ticket into a macro or into something your seat can decide next time.

quiz.prompt: Three weeks into the month, Analyn's client asks her to also watch the Instagram DMs. "Konti lang naman." She currently covers email and the page inbox inside an agreed window.

options.text: Agree, then say what the extra messages come to a day and what that does to email, and let the client choose
Say yes and absorb it quietly for now, and then raise it at month end if the extra messages turn out to be heavy
Agree for a trial month, then bring the client a proposal for a higher rate once she can show the channel is real
Decline until the agreement is rewritten, since the channels were all settled in writing before her first shift

quiz.explanation: Neither refuse nor absorb. A second channel is real work inside the same hours, so name what it costs and put the choice back where the authority sits: extend the window, drop something, or let email run slower. The count is what a queue adds to that move, and without it this is a complaint. A trial month leaves the email queue slipping for a month with nobody told.

quiz.prompt: You decide to pull ten of your own sent replies once a week and read them cold. What are you reading them for?

options.text: Typos, clumsy sentences and anything that reads awkwardly, since that is what a client notices when he opens up a transcript
Whether the first line answered the ask, whether every fact was checked, and whether anything was promised above your seat
The ones you are proudest of, so that the best of them can go straight into the sample pack you show a hiring client
Which of them a macro could have answered, so that the library grows out of what you actually typed by hand that week

quiz.explanation: The rubric is five questions and none of them is about polish: did the first line answer the ask, was every fact checked, did it promise only what your seat may grant, does it say what happens next and when, and would you be comfortable if the client read it aloud. It needs nobody's permission and no tool, which is why it is the cheapest improvement you have. The pack and the library are by-products.

quiz.prompt: Nico has run the booking inbox for a dental clinic in Davao for eight months. His application says "excellent communication skills, hardworking, fast learner". What would improve it fastest?

options.text: Add a line with his average first reply time from memory, since he worked that inbox every single day for eight months
Name the clinic, the eight months and the channels he covered, and give his best remembered figure for daily ticket volume
Ask the clinic owner for a reference letter and lead with that instead of describing the work himself
Attach a triage sheet, two macros, one hard reply and an escalation note, with names and numbers stripped out

quiz.explanation: Adjectives cannot be checked and every applicant has the same ones. Artefacts can be read in five minutes and show how he actually works. Naming the clinic and the months is a real improvement, and then it attaches a remembered figure, which fails the three part rule: what it counts, the window it covers, and where he got it. A reference letter says what somebody else thinks rather than what he did.

quiz.prompt: A hiring client sends one test: an angry customer demanding a refund on a late order, and the reply their own AI tool drafted for it. They ask what you would send. What does the strongest answer do?

options.text: Rewrite the draft from scratch in your own voice, so they can see that you do not need their tool to produce a reply at all
Keep the draft's structure and tone and correct only the facts, since the tool has handled the part they are testing
Send the draft back with the unconfirmed date and the refund promise cut, answer the request, and name what you assumed
Send the draft as it stands with a note listing the three things you would want checked before a real customer saw it

quiz.explanation: They are watching you edit. The draft is there because they want to see what you take out, so cutting the date nobody confirmed and the refund nobody authorised is the answer, along with the line naming your assumption about the policy. Rewriting from scratch hides the edit they asked to see, correcting only the facts leaves a promise standing, and a list of checks you did not run is not a reply.

assignment.title: The support pack for one real queue
assignment.brief_mdx:
Pick one support queue you could plausibly run: a Philippine online store, a small software product, a service business with a booking inbox, a clinic whose messages pile up all day. A real one is better. A realistic one you know well is fine. Then submit one text document with a short setup and five artefacts.

**The setup.** One paragraph. What the business sells, which channels customers write in on, what those customers usually want, and what one shift on this queue looks like.

Then the five artefacts.

1. **The triage sheet.** Your category set for this queue, short and fixed. The rule for what gets answered first, written so someone covering your shift would sort the same way you do. Then a two column list: what this seat may decide on its own, and what has to go to somebody else. At least one thing you would like to be able to grant has to sit on the escalate side, with the holding sentence you would send instead.

2. **Three macros.** Take three situations this queue would really see again and again. Write the reply for each with the variable slots marked, so a rushed agent cannot send one half filled. Show one of them filled in for a specific customer. No macro may state a policy, a fee, a delivery window or any figure you have not confirmed with the business.

3. **Three hard tickets.** One angry customer, one request you have to refuse, one you have to escalate. For each, give the ticket in a line or two, the AI draft, the version you would actually send, and one line naming what you changed and why. The change has to be a real change, not a note that the draft was fine.

4. **The unreviewed send rule sheet.** One page for this queue. What never reaches a customer without a human reading it first, written as concrete categories for this business rather than a general line about checking AI output. Include what happens on the morning the queue is backed up and the rule is inconvenient, because that is the morning it breaks.

5. **The coverage and authority statement, plus one escalation note.** What you would agree with the client before your first shift: which channels, which hours, roughly what volume, and what happens when the queue goes above it. Then the escalation note that travels with the ticket you escalated in part 3, written so the next person can act without reopening the whole thing.

Everything is text. No screenshots and no uploads. Replace real customer names, order numbers, phone numbers and email addresses before you submit. Do not state a fee, a commission, a refund timeline, a response time benchmark or a marketplace rule as fact anywhere in the pack. Where your queue needs one of those, write the placeholder and name who you would ask for the current answer. Doing that properly is part of what is being marked.
criteria: The triage sheet is specific to this business: every category traces to a ticket this queue would really receive, and the first-answered rule is written clearly enough that a colleague covering the shift would sort the same way

The authority split is real rather than decorative: at least one thing the learner clearly wants to grant sits on the escalate side with the holding sentence they would send instead, and the coverage statement names channels, hours, expected volume and what happens above it

The three macros are shaped around situations rather than individual customers, every variable slot is marked, one is shown filled in for a named case, and no macro states a policy, fee or timeframe the learner invented

Each hard reply answers the request first and promises nothing outside the stated authority, the named edit to the AI draft is a genuine change, and the escalation note gives the next person what was asked, what the customer has already been told, what was checked and what was promised

The unreviewed send rule sheet names concrete categories for this queue, covering money, dates, a customer's personal details and anyone who has already escalated, and says what holds when the queue is backed up, rather than restating that AI output should be checked

Real customer names, order numbers and contact details are removed or replaced, and no price, fee, refund timeline, response time benchmark or platform rule appears as a stated fact anywhere in the pack
